claim: Renal medullary carcinoma (RMC) was first identified in 1995 and is described as the seventh nephropathy of sickle cell disease.
source: Renal medullary carcinoma (RMC) was first identified in 1995 and is described as the seventh nephropathy of sickle cell disease (Davis et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Davis et al., 1995, which provides historical documentation of RMC identification and classification.

claim: RMC is a rare cancer that occurs primarily in patients of African descent that carry sickle cell trait.
source: RMC is a rare cancer that occurs primarily in patients of African descent that carry sickle cell trait and presents during adolescence with symptoms of abdominal pain, hematuria, weight loss and widely metastatic disease.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about RMC's epidemiology and clinical presentation.

claim: RMC presents during adolescence with symptoms of abdominal pain, hematuria, weight loss and widely metastatic disease.
source: RMC is a rare cancer that occurs primarily in patients of African descent that carry sickle cell trait and presents during adolescence with symptoms of abdominal pain, hematuria, weight loss and widely metastatic disease.
evidence: This describes the clinical presentation of RMC based on established medical knowledge.

claim: The mean overall survival rate for RMC patients is only 6–8 months despite aggressive multimodal therapy.
source: Despite this aggressive regimen, the mean overall survival rate is only 6–8 months (Alvarez et al., 2015; Beckermann et al., 2017; Ezekian et al., 2017; Iacovelli et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations documenting survival outcomes in RMC patients.

claim: Recent studies have implicated loss of SMARCB1 in RMC.
source: Recent studies have implicated loss of SMARCB1 in RMC (Calderaro et al., 2016; Carlo et al., 2017; Cheng et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies that have identified SMARCB1 loss in RMC.

claim: SMARCB1 is a tumor suppressor that when conditionally inactivated in mice leads to rapid onset of lymphomas or brain tumors.
source: SMARCB1 is a tumor suppressor that when conditionally inactivated in mice leads to rapid onset of lymphomas or brain tumors (Han et al., 2016; Roberts et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating the tumor suppressor function of SMARCB1 in mouse models.

claim: SMARCB1 is a core member of the SWI/SNF complex.
source: Furthermore, SMARCB1 is a core member of the SWI/SNF complex where alterations of one or more members have been identified in up to 20% of all cancers (Helming et al., 2014; Kadoch et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations documenting SMARCB1's role in the SWI/SNF complex.

claim: Alterations of one or more SWI/SNF complex members have been identified in up to 20% of all cancers.
source: Furthermore, SMARCB1 is a core member of the SWI/SNF complex where alterations of one or more members have been identified in up to 20% of all cancers (Helming et al., 2014; Kadoch et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations documenting the frequency of SWI/SNF alterations across cancers.

claim: MRTs and ATRTs harbor few somatic genetic alterations other than biallelic loss of SMARCB1 and occur in young children.
source: MRTs and ATRTs harbor few somatic genetic alterations other than biallelic loss of SMARCB1 and occur in young children (Chun et al., 2016; Gröbner et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2012; Ma et al., 2018; Torchia et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations documenting the genomic landscape and age of onset of MRTs and ATRTs.

claim: RMC patients present as adolescents/young adults and are primarily of African descent.
source: In contrast, RMC patients present as adolescents/young adults, are primarily of African descent and have been found to have fusion events in SMARCB1 and gene mutations in ERG, PDGFRB, MTOR, and ERBB2 (Calderaro et al., 2016; Carlo et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations documenting the demographics and genomic features of RMC patients.

claim: RMC patients have been found to have fusion events in SMARCB1 and gene mutations in ERG, PDGFRB, MTOR, and ERBB2.
source: In contrast, RMC patients present as adolescents/young adults, are primarily of African descent and have been found to have fusion events in SMARCB1 and gene mutations in ERG, PDGFRB, MTOR, and ERBB2 (Calderaro et al., 2016; Carlo et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations documenting the genomic alterations found in RMC patients.

claim: Cell lines were generated from two of the three RMC patients (CLF_PEDS0005 and CLF_PEDS9001).
source: We then attempted to develop cell lines from these patients and generated cell lines from two of the three patients (CLF_PEDS0005 and CLF_PEDS9001) (Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the derivation of cell lines from patient samples.

claim: For patient CLF_PEDS0005, a normal kidney cell line (CLF_PEDS0005_N) and a tumor cell line (CLF_PEDS0005_T1) were generated from the primary tissue.
source: We generated a short-term culture normal kidney cell line, CLF_PEDS0005_N, and a tumor cell line, CLF_PEDS0005_T1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and references a figure showing the derivation process.

claim: Two additional cell lines (CLF_PEDS0005_T2A and CLF_PEDS0005_T2B) were isolated from pleural fluid obtained when patient CLF_PEDS0005 relapsed 8 months into therapy.
source: In addition, we obtained fluid from a thoracentesis performed when the patient relapsed 8 months into therapy. We isolated two cell lines that grew either as an adherent monolayer, CLF_PEDS0005_T2A, or in suspension, CLF_PEDS0005_T2B.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the derivation of metastatic cell lines.

claim: RMC tumor cell lines expressed the epithelial marker CAM5.2 and lacked expression of SMARCB1 similar to that observed in the primary tumor.
source: Each of these tumor cell lines expressed the epithelial marker, CAM5.2, and lacked expression of SMARCB1 similar to that observed in the primary tumor (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Cell lines were generated from patients who received 4–8 weeks of neoadjuvant chemotherapy prior to their nephrectomy.
source: Cell lines were generated from patients who received 4–8 weeks of neoadjuvant chemotherapy prior to their nephrectomy.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the clinical context of sample collection.

claim: WES and WGS confirmed the presence of sickle cell trait in both RMC patients.
source: In both patients, we confirmed the presence of sickle cell trait but also found tumor purity was <20%, which, like prior studies, prevented the identification of the fusion events (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing data showing the sickle cell trait mutation in the hemoglobin beta gene.

claim: Tumor purity in primary RMC tissue samples was <20%, which prevented the identification of fusion events.
source: In both patients, we confirmed the presence of sickle cell trait but also found tumor purity was <20%, which, like prior studies, prevented the identification of the fusion events (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is based on sequencing data analysis showing low tumor purity in tissue samples.

claim: RMC tumor cell lines had a low mutation frequency (1–3 mutations/mb) similar to other pediatric cancers.
source: We found a low mutation frequency (1–3 mutations/mb; Materials and methods; Figure 1a) in the tumor cell lines similar to that of other pediatric cancers and cell lines such as MRT, ATRT and Ewing sarcoma (Cibulskis et al., 2013; Johann et al., 2016; Wala et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by WES data showing mutation rates and citations comparing to other pediatric cancers.

claim: Only the metastatic RMC cell lines harbored mutations in TP53 and TPR.
source: We found that only the metastatic cell lines harbored mutations in TP53 and TPR (Materials and methods; Supplementary file 1) (Cibulskis et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on WES data analysis identifying mutations specific to metastatic cell lines.

claim: Copy number analysis confirmed heterozygous loss of SMARCB1 in RMC cell lines.
source: Using copy number analysis, we confirmed the heterozygous loss of SMARCB1.
evidence: The claim is supported by copy number analysis from sequencing data.

claim: WES failed to identify an identifiable mutation or deletion to account for the loss of the second SMARCB1 allele.
source: In agreement with prior studies, we failed to find an identifiable mutation or deletion to account for the loss of the second SMARCB1 allele with WES.
evidence: The claim is based on WES data analysis showing no detectable mutation or deletion in the second SMARCB1 allele.

claim: Dual-color break apart FISH identified a fusion event leading to loss of the second SMARCB1 allele in RMC cell lines.
source: We used dual-color break apart FISH and found that a fusion event led to loss of the second SMARCB1 allele as seen in prior studies (Materials and methods; Supplementary file 2) (Calderaro et al., 2016; Carlo et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH data showing SMARCB1 rearrangement and citations to prior studies.

claim: In CLF_PEDS0005_T1, one SMARCB1 allele was lost by a large deletion between BCR and MYH9.
source: For CLF_PEDS0005_T1, we found a large deletion between BCR and MYH9 which is predicted to lead to loss of one allele of SMARCB1 (Figure 1c)
evidence: The claim is supported by WGS data showing a large deletion encompassing SMARCB1.

claim: In CLF_PEDS0005_T1, the second SMARCB1 allele was inactivated by a balanced translocation between intron 1 of SMARCB1 and the C-terminal end of C1orf116.
source: along with a balanced translocation between intron 1 of SMARCB1 to the intron region following the C-terminal end of C1orf116, yielding a non-functional allele (Figure 1d and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by WGS data showing the specific translocation breakpoint.

claim: In CLF_PEDS9001_T1, one SMARCB1 allele was lost by a large deletion between TTC28 and VPREB.
source: For CLF_PEDS9001_T1, we found a large deletion between TTC28 and VPREB that would lead to loss of one allele of SMARCB1 (Figure 1e)
evidence: The claim is supported by WGS data showing a large deletion encompassing SMARCB1.

claim: In CLF_PEDS9001_T1, the second SMARCB1 allele was inactivated by a balanced translocation between intron 10 of PLEKHA5 and intron 6 of SMARCB1.
source: along with a balanced translocation that leads to fusion of intron 10 of PLEKHA5 to intron 6 of SMARCB1 (Figure 1f and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by WGS data showing the specific translocation breakpoint.

claim: Both SMARCB1 translocations in RMC cell lines involved inactivation of the C-terminal end of SMARCB1.
source: Both translocations involved inactivation of the C-terminal end of SMARCB1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the translocation breakpoints relative to SMARCB1 protein domains.

claim: SMARCB1 fusion breakpoints were confirmed by Sanger sequencing, qRT-PCR, and immunoblotting.
source: We confirmed these findings by Sanger sequencing of the breakpoint, by qRT-PCR and by immunoblotting to demonstrate loss of SMARCB1 expression (Supplementary file 5, Figure 1—figure supplement 1e–f; Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple orthogonal validation methods confirming the genomic findings.

claim: No alignments, fragile sites, or repetitive DNA elements were shared among SMARCB1 breakpoint sequences from different RMC cases.
source: We then assessed previously identified breakpoint SMARCB1 sequences with the breakpoints identified in this study and failed to find alignments, fragile sites or other repetitive DNA elements that were shared amongst these sequences (Figure 1—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis comparing breakpoints across multiple RMC cases.

claim: RMC cell lines clustered with TARGET Rhabdoid Tumor samples by tSNE analysis of RNA-sequencing data.
source: The normal cell line, CLF_PEDS0005_N, clustered with TARGET normal kidney tissues and RMC cell lines from both patients clustered with the TARGET Rhabdoid Tumor samples (Figure 2a).
evidence: The claim is supported by tSNE analysis of RNA-sequencing data comparing RMC to other pediatric renal tumors.

claim: RMC cell lines share expression patterns with patients with MRTs.
source: These observations showed that these RMC cell lines share expression patterns with patients with MRTs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the tSNE clustering analysis showing RMC cell lines grouping with MRT samples.

claim: RMC cell lines clustered with RMC patients and MRT/ATRT samples by tSNE analysis of gene expression array data.
source: Using tSNE, we found that the RMC cell lines closely mapped to a French cohort of RMC, MRT and ATRT patients (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by tSNE analysis of gene expression array data comparing RMC cell lines to patient samples.

claim: In SMARCB1 wild-type HA1E cells, SWI/SNF complex members SMARCB1, ARID1A and SMARCA4 were robustly expressed at higher molecular weights in glycerol gradients.
source: In HA1E SMARCB1 wild-type cells, the SWI/SNF complex members SMARCB1, ARID1A and SMARCA4 were robustly expressed at higher molecular weights (e.g. fractions 13–16).
evidence: The claim is based on glycerol gradient sedimentation data showing the distribution of SWI/SNF complex members.

claim: In SMARCB1 deficient G401 cells, the SWI/SNF complex is smaller and seen at lower molecular weights in glycerol gradients.
source: In G401 SMARCB1 deficient cells, the SWI/SNF complex is smaller and seen at lower molecular weights (e.g. fractions 10–14).
evidence: The claim is based on glycerol gradient sedimentation data showing altered SWI/SNF complex size in SMARCB1-deficient cells.

claim: Expression of SWI/SNF complex members was modestly decreased in SMARCB1-deficient G401 cells.
source: Furthermore, expression of SWI/SNF complex members was modestly decreased in G401, consistent with our prior studies (Nakayama et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on glycerol gradient data and supported by citations to prior studies showing similar findings.

claim: Re-expression of SMARCB1 in RMC cell lines led to increased expression and a shift of ARID1A and SMARCA4 to larger fractions in glycerol gradients.
source: In addition, we found increased expression and a shift of ARID1A and SMARCA4 to larger fractions 13–15 upon re-expression of SMARCB1 in the RMC lines similar to what we observed in the SMARCB1 wild-type HA1E cell line.
evidence: The claim is based on glycerol gradient sedimentation data comparing SMARCB1-deficient and SMARCB1-restored RMC cells.

claim: The composition of the SWI/SNF complex is similar between RMC and other SMARCB1 deficient cancers.
source: We concluded that the composition of the SWI/SNF complex is similar between RMC and other SMARCB1 deficient cancers.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the glycerol gradient data showing similar SWI/SNF complex behavior in RMC and MRT cells.

claim: Induction of SMARCB1 in HA1E SMARCB1 wild-type cells showed no significant difference in viability compared to LacZ control.
source: In the HA1E SMARCB1 wild type cells, we found no significant difference in viability between induction of SMARCB1 versus induction of LacZ using direct counting of viable cells (Figure 2e).
evidence: The claim is based on cell viability assays comparing SMARCB1 and LacZ induction in wild-type cells.

claim: Induction of SMARCB1 in SMARCB1-deficient G401 cells decreased the number of viable cells by 41%.
source: In contrast, induction of SMARCB1 in the MRT G401 SMARCB1 deficient cells decreased the number of viable cells by 41%.
evidence: The claim is based on cell viability assays showing decreased viability upon SMARCB1 re-expression in MRT cells.

claim: Re-expression of SMARCB1 in RMC models led to significant decreases in cell viability (37–62%).
source: Similar to G401, we found that re-expression of SMARCB1 in each of the RMC models led to significant decreases in cell viability (37–62%) (Figure 2e; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is based on cell viability assays showing decreased viability upon SMARCB1 re-expression in RMC cells.

claim: Loss of SMARCB1 is required for the proliferation and viability of RMC cells.
source: These observations suggest loss of SMARCB1 is required for the proliferation and viability of RMC cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the viability data showing that SMARCB1 re-expression decreases RMC cell viability.

claim: 44.6% (±17%) of RMC cells stained for β-galactosidase when SMARCB1 was expressed, indicating senescence.
source: We failed to observe cells expressing β-galactosidase upon expression of LacZ in the RMC cells, but when SMARCB1 was expressed, we found 44.6% (±17%) of the RMC cells stained for β-galactosidase (Figure 2f and Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: The claim is based on senescence-associated β-galactosidase staining assays in RMC cells with SMARCB1 re-expression.

claim: Re-expression of SMARCB1 in RMC cells may lead to senescence.
source: These studies showed that re-expression of SMARCB1 in RMC cells may also lead to senescence.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the β-galactosidase staining data showing senescence markers upon SMARCB1 re-expression.

claim: 1719 genes were significantly different (FDR < 0.25) upon SMARCB1 re-expression in RMC cells.
source: We found 1719 genes to be significantly different (false discovery rate of <0.25) in the RMC cells and 2735 genes in MRT cells.
evidence: The claim is based on RNA-sequencing data analysis comparing SMARCB1-deficient and SMARCB1-restored RMC cells.

claim: 2735 genes were significantly different (FDR < 0.25) upon SMARCB1 re-expression in MRT cells.
source: We found 1719 genes to be significantly different (false discovery rate of <0.25) in the RMC cells and 2735 genes in MRT cells.
evidence: The claim is based on RNA-sequencing data analysis comparing SMARCB1-deficient and SMARCB1-restored MRT cells.

claim: 527 genes significantly overlapped between RMC and MRT cells upon SMARCB1 re-expression (hypergeometric p-value < 4.035e-63).
source: We identified 527 genes that significantly overlapped between the RMC and MRT cell lines (hypergeometric p-value less than 4.035e-63; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of RNA-sequencing data comparing differentially expressed genes in RMC and MRT cells.

claim: 257 genes overlapped between the 527 differentially expressed genes upon SMARCB1 re-expression and genes differentially expressed between MRT tumor and normal tissues.
source: We compared this group of genes to the genes differentially expressed between MRT tumor and normal tissues from TARGET (n = 6,311). We identified 257 genes that overlapped with the 527 significantly differentially expressed genes induced by re-expression of SMARCB1 (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: The claim is based on comparative analysis of gene expression data from multiple sources.

claim: Gene ontology analysis of 257 genes identified significantly enriched gene sets related to the cell cycle and the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
source: Using this list of 257 genes, we performed gene ontology (GO)-based Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) (Subramanian et al., 2005) and identified significantly enriched genes sets (q-value <0.1), including those related to the cell cycle and the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS).
evidence: The claim is based on GSEA analysis of differentially expressed genes upon SMARCB1 re-expression.

claim: PLK1 and CCNB1 showed a gradual decrease in expression over 120 hr after SMARCB1 re-expression.
source: For PLK1 and CCNB1, we observed a gradual decrease in expression over the course of 120 hr whereas RRM2, UBE2C and TOP2A exhibited a more profound decrease in expression after the first 24 hr and then a modest decrease over the following 96 hr (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e–f).
evidence: The claim is based on time-course RNA-sequencing data tracking gene expression changes after SMARCB1 re-expression.

claim: RRM2, UBE2C and TOP2A exhibited a more profound decrease in expression after the first 24 hr following SMARCB1 re-expression.
source: For PLK1 and CCNB1, we observed a gradual decrease in expression over the course of 120 hr whereas RRM2, UBE2C and TOP2A exhibited a more profound decrease in expression after the first 24 hr and then a modest decrease over the following 96 hr (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e–f).
evidence: The claim is based on time-course RNA-sequencing data tracking gene expression changes after SMARCB1 re-expression.

claim: Changes in the transcriptome following SMARCB1 re-expression in RMC cell lines are similar to other SMARCB1 deficient cancer cell lines.
source: These findings confirm that changes in the transcriptome following SMARCB1 re-expression in RMC cell lines are similar to other SMARCB1 deficient cancer cell lines.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparative analysis of gene expression changes in RMC and MRT cells upon SMARCB1 re-expression.

claim: RMC cell lines are functionally similar to those derived from other SMARCB1 deficient cancers.
source: In sum, these observations indicate that the RMC cell lines are functionally similar to those derived from other SMARCB1 deficient cancers.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple lines of evidence including transcriptome analysis, SWI/SNF complex composition, and viability assays.

claim: 72 genes scored with a RIGER p-value<0.05 in CLF_PEDS0005_T2A RNAi screen.
source: Of 444 evaluable genes, 72 genes scored with a RIGER p-value<0.05 in CLF_PEDS0005_T2A and 74 genes scored in CLF_PEDS0005_T2B.
evidence: The claim is based on RNAi screen data analyzed using the RIGER algorithm.

claim: 74 genes scored with a RIGER p-value<0.05 in CLF_PEDS0005_T2B RNAi screen.
source: Of 444 evaluable genes, 72 genes scored with a RIGER p-value<0.05 in CLF_PEDS0005_T2A and 74 genes scored in CLF_PEDS0005_T2B.
evidence: The claim is based on RNAi screen data analyzed using the RIGER algorithm.

claim: 124 genes scored with a RIGER p-value<0.05 in CLF_PEDS0005_T2A CRISPR-Cas9 screen.
source: We used RIGER to collapse the individual sgRNAs to consensus gene dependencies and found 124 genes (of a total of 445 evaluable genes) and 136 genes (of a total of 445 evaluable genes) with a RIGER p-value<0.05 in CLF_PEDS0005_T2A and CLF_PEDS0005_T2B cell lines, respectively.
evidence: The claim is based on CRISPR-Cas9 screen data analyzed using the RIGER algorithm.

claim: 136 genes scored with a RIGER p-value<0.05 in CLF_PEDS0005_T2B CRISPR-Cas9 screen.
source: We used RIGER to collapse the individual sgRNAs to consensus gene dependencies and found 124 genes (of a total of 445 evaluable genes) and 136 genes (of a total of 445 evaluable genes) with a RIGER p-value<0.05 in CLF_PEDS0005_T2A and CLF_PEDS0005_T2B cell lines, respectively.
evidence: The claim is based on CRISPR-Cas9 screen data analyzed using the RIGER algorithm.

claim: 75 compounds (18%) significantly decreased cell viability (AUC < 0.5) in CLF_PEDS0005_T2A small-molecule screen.
source: Of the evaluable compounds, 75 (18%) compounds significantly decreased cell viability in CLF_PEDS0005_T2A and 82 (20%) compounds significantly decreased cell viability in CLF_PEDS0005_T2B.
evidence: The claim is based on small-molecule screening data measuring cell viability.

claim: 82 compounds (20%) significantly decreased cell viability (AUC < 0.5) in CLF_PEDS0005_T2B small-molecule screen.
source: Of the evaluable compounds, 75 (18%) compounds significantly decreased cell viability in CLF_PEDS0005_T2A and 82 (20%) compounds significantly decreased cell viability in CLF_PEDS0005_T2B.
evidence: The claim is based on small-molecule screening data measuring cell viability.

claim: 21 genes scored in all three screens (RNAi, CRISPR-Cas9, and small-molecule) in CLF_PEDS0005_T2A.
source: We identified 21 genes in CLF_PEDS0005_T2A and 27 genes in CLF_PEDS0005_T2B (Supplementary file 7) of which 19 genes scored in both screens (Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is based on integration of data from three orthogonal screening approaches.

claim: 27 genes scored in all three screens (RNAi, CRISPR-Cas9, and small-molecule) in CLF_PEDS0005_T2B.
source: We identified 21 genes in CLF_PEDS0005_T2A and 27 genes in CLF_PEDS0005_T2B (Supplementary file 7) of which 19 genes scored in both screens (Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is based on integration of data from three orthogonal screening approaches.

claim: 19 genes scored in all three screens in both CLF_PEDS0005_T2A and CLF_PEDS0005_T2B.
source: We identified 21 genes in CLF_PEDS0005_T2A and 27 genes in CLF_PEDS0005_T2B (Supplementary file 7) of which 19 genes scored in both screens (Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is based on integration of data from three orthogonal screening approaches across both cell lines.

claim: The 19 overlapping genes include components of the ubiquitin-proteasome system (PSMB1, PSMB2, PSMB5, PSMD1, PSMD2, and CUL1).
source: Among the 19 genes were components of the ubiquitin-proteasome system (e.g. PSMB1, PSMB2, PSMB5, PSMD1, PSMD2, and CUL1), regulators of the cell cycle (CDK1, CDK6, KIF11 and PLK1) and genes involved in nuclear export (KPNB1 and XPO1).
evidence: The claim is based on functional annotation of genes identified in the integrated screen analysis.

claim: The 19 overlapping genes include regulators of the cell cycle (CDK1, CDK6, KIF11 and PLK1).
source: Among the 19 genes were components of the ubiquitin-proteasome system (e.g. PSMB1, PSMB2, PSMB5, PSMD1, PSMD2, and CUL1), regulators of the cell cycle (CDK1, CDK6, KIF11 and PLK1) and genes involved in nuclear export (KPNB1 and XPO1).
evidence: The claim is based on functional annotation of genes identified in the integrated screen analysis.

claim: The 19 overlapping genes include genes involved in nuclear export (KPNB1 and XPO1).
source: Among the 19 genes were components of the ubiquitin-proteasome system (e.g. PSMB1, PSMB2, PSMB5, PSMD1, PSMD2, and CUL1), regulators of the cell cycle (CDK1, CDK6, KIF11 and PLK1) and genes involved in nuclear export (KPNB1 and XPO1).
evidence: The claim is based on functional annotation of genes identified in the integrated screen analysis.

claim: RMC tumor cells were differentially sensitive (up to two standard deviations) to proteasome inhibitors bortezomib and MLN2238 compared to the normal cell line.
source: We found that the tumor cells were differentially sensitive (up to two standard deviations) upon treatment with proteasome inhibitors, bortezomib and MLN2238, when compared to the normal cell line (Figure 3b; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is based on small-molecule screening data comparing tumor and normal cell lines.

claim: The vulnerability to proteasome inhibition may be dependent on loss of SMARCB1.
source: These findings suggest that the vulnerability to proteasome inhibition may be dependent on loss of SMARCB1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential sensitivity to proteasome inhibitors between SMARCB1-deficient tumor cells and SMARCB1-expressing normal cells.

claim: Deletion of proteasome components affected the RMC model CLF_PEDS0005_T1 to a statistically greater degree than the undifferentiated sarcoma model CLF_PEDS015T (two-tailed t-test p=7.1e-8).
source: Although deletion of the proteasome members affected proliferation in all of the models (two tailed t-test p=1.1e-5 for CLF_PEDS015T and p=5.4e-20 for CLF_PEDS0005_T1), we found that suppression of proteasome components affected the RMC model CLF_PEDS0005_T1 to a statistically greater degree (two tailed t-test p=7.1e-8).
evidence: The claim is based on CRISPR-Cas9 deletion data comparing the effects of proteasome deletion in RMC versus non-SMARCB1-deficient cells.

claim: Gene deletion of PSMB5 by CRISPR-Cas9 in CLF_PEDS0005_T2A and CLF_PEDS9001_T1 cell lines led to decreased viability.
source: We subsequently validated that gene deletion by CRISPR-Cas9 of PSMB5, one of the primary targets of proteasome inhibitors, in the CLF_PEDS0005_T2A and CLF_PEDS9001_T1 cell lines led to decreased viability (Figure 3—figure supplement 1h–i).
evidence: The claim is based on CRISPR-Cas9 validation experiments measuring cell viability after PSMB5 deletion.

claim: SMARCB1-retained isogenic cell lines showed significantly decreased sensitivity to proteasome inhibitors compared to SMARCB1-deficient cell lines.
source: We observed significantly decreased sensitivity to the proteasome inhibitors in the SMARCB1 retained isogenic cell lines as compared to the SMARCB1 deficient cell lines (Figure 3d–e).
evidence: The claim is based on dose-response experiments comparing SMARCB1-expressing and SMARCB1-deficient isogenic cell lines.

claim: Re-expression of SMARCB1 led to a decrease in sensitivity to bortezomib or MLN2238 compared to isogenic SMARCB1-deficient lines.
source: We then treated our SMARCB1-inducible RMC and MRT cell lines with DMSO, bortezomib or MLN2238. Re-expression of SMARCB1 led to a decrease in sensitivity to bortezomib or MLN2238 as compared to the isogenic SMARCB1 deficient lines (Figure 3f–g).
evidence: The claim is based on dose-response experiments in inducible SMARCB1 cell lines.

claim: The differential resistance to SMARCB1 re-expression was between 2–3-fold with either bortezomib or MLN2238.
source: The observed differential resistance to SMARCB1 re-expression was between 2–3-fold with either bortezomib or MLN2238 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–b).
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative analysis of dose-response data in inducible SMARCB1 cell lines.

claim: Re-expression of SMARCB1 partially rescued the sensitivity of MRT or RMC cell lines to proteasome inhibition.
source: We concluded that re-expression of SMARCB1 partially rescued the sensitivity of MRT or RMC cell lines to proteasome inhibition.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the dose-response data showing decreased sensitivity upon SMARCB1 re-expression.

claim: SMARCB1-deficient cell lines were significantly more sensitive (two-tailed t-test p-value=0.011) to treatment with MLN2238 than non-multiple myeloma CCLE cell lines.
source: We found that SMARCB1-deficient cell lines were significantly more sensitive (two-tailed t-test p-value=0.011) to treatment with MLN2238 than non-multiple myeloma CCLE cell lines (Figure 4a; Figure 4—source data 1) (Rees et al., 2016; Seashore-Ludlow et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of CCLE small-molecule screening data comparing SMARCB1-deficient cell lines to other cancer cell lines.

claim: The degree of sensitivity of SMARCB1-deficient cell lines to MLN2238 was similar to that of multiple myeloma cell lines.
source: The degree of sensitivity was similar to that of multiple myeloma cell lines which are known to be sensitive to proteasome inhibition (Dimopoulos et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on comparative analysis of CCLE screening data and supported by citation to multiple myeloma literature.

claim: SMARCB1-deficient cell lines are selectively vulnerable to proteasome inhibition.
source: These findings confirm that SMARCB1 deficient cell lines are selectively vulnerable to proteasome inhibition.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the CCLE analysis showing preferential sensitivity of SMARCB1-deficient cell lines to proteasome inhibitors.

claim: SMARCB1-deficient cell lines exhibited single digit nanomolar sensitivity to bortezomib similar to multiple myeloma cell line RPMI8226.
source: We found that our SMARCB1 deficient cell lines exhibited single digit nanomolar sensitivity to proteasome inhibition similar to that observed in the multiple myeloma cell line RPMI8226 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is based on dose-response experiments comparing SMARCB1-deficient cell lines to multiple myeloma and lung cancer cell lines.

claim: The IC50 of bortezomib in H2172 lung cancer cell line was at least 3-fold higher than in SMARCB1-deficient cell lines.
source: In contrast, we found that the IC50 in H2172 was at least 3-fold higher.
evidence: The claim is based on dose-response experiments comparing SMARCB1-deficient cell lines to a non-sensitive control cell line.

claim: Wilms tumor cell line CLF_PEDS1012_T was more resistant to proteasome inhibition compared to RMC models and MRT cell line G401.
source: We found that CLF_PEDS1012_T was more resistant to proteasome inhibition as compared to our RMC models and MRT cell line, G401.
evidence: The claim is based on dose-response experiments comparing SMARCB1-wildtype Wilms tumor cells to SMARCB1-deficient RMC and MRT cells.

claim: SMARCB1-deficient cells are more sensitive to proteasome inhibition.
source: These findings suggest that SMARCB1-deficient cells are more sensitive to proteasome inhibition.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple dose-response experiments comparing SMARCB1-deficient and SMARCB1-wildtype cells.

claim: Treatment with bortezomib or MLN2238 did not suppress c-MYC protein levels in SMARCB1-deficient RMC and MRT cell lines.
source: Compared to RPMI8226, a multiple myeloma cell line that relies on c-MYC for survival (Tagde et al., 2016), we failed to observe suppression of c-MYC protein levels following bortezomib or MLN2238 treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: The claim is based on immunoblot data measuring c-MYC protein levels after proteasome inhibitor treatment.

claim: c-MYC expression levels were increased after MLN2238 treatment in G401, CLF_PEDS9001T, and CLF_PEDS00005_T1 cell lines.
source: We then assessed c-MYC expression levels in the G401, CLF_PEDS9001T, and CLF_PEDS00005_T1 cell lines following treatment with MLN2238 and found that c-MYC levels were increased after MLN2238 treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: The claim is based on RNA-sequencing data measuring c-MYC transcript levels after proteasome inhibitor treatment.

claim: Proteasome inhibition in SMARCB1-deficient RMC and MRT models does not lead to suppression of c-MYC.
source: In our models of RMC and MRT, these findings suggest proteasome inhibition does not lead to suppression of c-MYC.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the c-MYC protein and transcript data showing no decrease upon proteasome inhibition.

claim: No consistent significant change in total or nuclear protein levels of SWI/SNF complex members was observed upon treatment with a proteasome inhibitor.
source: We failed to see a consistent significant change in total or nuclear protein when immunoblotting for SWI/SNF complex members (SMARCE1, SMARCD1, SMARCD1, SMARCC1, SMARCC2, SMARCA4 and ARID1A) other than increases in SMARCB1 levels upon doxycycline treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a–b).
evidence: The claim is based on immunoblot data from subcellular fractionation experiments after proteasome inhibitor treatment.

claim: Inhibition of the proteasome in SMARCB1-deficient cancers does not alter the total or nuclear levels of SWI/SNF complex members.
source: These findings suggest that inhibition of the proteasome in SMARCB1 deficient cancers and its subsequent resistance upon SMARCB1 expression does not alter the total or nuclear levels of SWI/SNF complex members.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the immunoblot data showing no change in SWI/SNF complex member levels upon proteasome inhibition.

claim: ER stress markers GRP78 and IRE1α increased following treatment with MLN2238.
source: We saw an increase in protein expression of markers of ER stress, GRP78 and IRE1α, following treatment with MLN2238 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: The claim is based on immunoblot data measuring ER stress markers after proteasome inhibitor treatment.

claim: ER stress markers GRP78 and IRE1α were not rescued by SMARCB1 re-expression upon proteasome inhibitor treatment.
source: Upon re-expression of SMARCB1 and subsequent treatment with a proteasome inhibitor, we did not see changes in either GRP78 or IRE1α protein levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: The claim is based on immunoblot data comparing ER stress markers in SMARCB1-deficient and SMARCB1-restored cells after proteasome inhibition.

claim: ER stress markers are elevated upon proteasome inhibition in SMARCB1-deficient cell lines but are not rescued by SMARCB1 re-expression.
source: These observations suggest that although ER stress markers are elevated upon proteasome inhibition in SMARCB1-deficient cell lines, they are not rescued by SMARCB1 re-expression.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the ER stress marker data showing elevation with proteasome inhibition but no change with SMARCB1 re-expression.

claim: GO-based GSEA identified numerous gene sets involving the ubiquitin-proteasome system among the 527 significantly altered genes upon SMARCB1 re-expression.
source: We then performed GO-based GSEA (Subramanian et al., 2005) on the 527 significantly altered genes upon re-expression of SMARCB1 (Supplementary file 6) to identify classes of gene function enriched in this group of genes. We identified numerous gene sets that involved the ubiquitin-proteasome system (Supplementary file 8).
evidence: The claim is based on GSEA analysis of differentially expressed genes upon SMARCB1 re-expression.

claim: 1758 genes were significantly (FDR < 0.1) up- or down-regulated upon treatment with MLN2238.
source: We then performed RNA-sequencing on G401 and the RMC cell lines treated with DMSO or MLN2238. We identified 1758 genes which were significantly (FDR < 0.1) up- or down-regulated upon treatment with MLN2238 (Supplementary file 9).
evidence: The claim is based on RNA-sequencing data comparing DMSO and MLN2238-treated cells.

claim: 92 genes overlapped between the 527 differentially expressed genes upon SMARCB1 re-expression and the 1758 differentially expressed genes upon MLN2238 treatment.
source: We compared the 527 differentially expressed genes identified upon re-expression of SMARCB1 with the 1758 differentially expressed genes identified upon treatment with MLN2238 and identified 92 genes which overlapped.
evidence: The claim is based on comparative analysis of gene expression data from SMARCB1 re-expression and proteasome inhibition experiments.

claim: 63 genes were differentially expressed with SMARCB1 re-expression and inversely differentially expressed with MLN2238 treatment.
source: Of these genes, we identified 63 genes which were differentially expressed with re-expression of SMARCB1 and were inversely differentially expressed with treatment with MLN2238 (Figure 4d; Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: The claim is based on comparative analysis of gene expression data showing opposite directional changes.

claim: GO-based GSEA of the 63 genes found significant enrichment (adjusted p-value 0 to 0.0061) in gene sets involving the cell cycle.
source: From this refined gene set, we performed GO-based GSEA (Subramanian et al., 2005) and found significant enrichment (adjusted p-value ranging from 0 to 0.0061) in gene sets involving the cell cycle (Supplementary file 10).
evidence: The claim is based on GSEA analysis of the refined set of genes showing opposite regulation by SMARCB1 and proteasome inhibition.

claim: Treatment with MLN2238 for 24 hr caused a significant shift of cells to G2/M (two-tailed t-test p-value 0.0005).
source: We observed a significant shift in cells to G2/M (two-tailed t-test p-value 0.0005; Figure 4e).
evidence: The claim is based on cell cycle analysis by flow cytometry after proteasome inhibitor treatment.

claim: Re-expression of SMARCB1 rescued the G2/M arrest phenotype caused by MLN2238 treatment.
source: Upon re-expression of SMARCB1, we saw that this phenotype was rescued (Figure 4f).
evidence: The claim is based on cell cycle analysis comparing SMARCB1-deficient and SMARCB1-restored cells after proteasome inhibitor treatment.

claim: By 48 hr after MLN2238 treatment, there was a significant increase in Annexin V and PI positive cells.
source: By 48 hr, we saw a significant increase in markers of programed cell death such as Annexin V and PI positive cells (Figure 4g).
evidence: The claim is based on flow cytometry analysis of apoptosis markers after proteasome inhibitor treatment.

claim: Treatment with a proteasome inhibitor led to increased cleaved caspase-3 levels.
source: We found that treatment with a proteasome inhibitor led to increased cleaved caspase-3 levels in addition to changes to Annexin V and PI, suggesting that inhibition of the ubiquitin-proteasome system leads to programmed cell death (Figure 4h).
evidence: The claim is based on immunoblot data showing cleaved caspase-3 activation after proteasome inhibitor treatment.

claim: Inhibition of the ubiquitin-proteasome system leads to programmed cell death.
source: We found that treatment with a proteasome inhibitor led to increased cleaved caspase-3 levels in addition to changes to Annexin V and PI, suggesting that inhibition of the ubiquitin-proteasome system leads to programmed cell death (Figure 4h).
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple markers of apoptosis (cleaved caspase-3, Annexin V, PI) observed after proteasome inhibition.

claim: Induction of cleaved caspase-3 was less pronounced when SMARCB1 was re-expressed.
source: We found that induction of cleaved caspase-3 was less pronounced when SMARCB1 was re-expressed (Figure 4h).
evidence: The claim is based on immunoblot data comparing cleaved caspase-3 levels in SMARCB1-deficient and SMARCB1-restored cells after proteasome inhibition.

claim: Proteasome inhibitors initially lead to a SMARCB1-dependent G2/M cell cycle arrest and subsequent programmed cell death.
source: These observations suggest that proteasome inhibitors initially lead to a SMARCB1-dependent G2/M cell cycle arrest and subsequent programmed cell death.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the cell cycle and apoptosis data showing G2/M arrest followed by cell death, both of which are modulated by SMARCB1 status.

claim: Treatment with nocodazole or RO-3306 for 24 hr caused accumulation of cells in G2/M and increased cyclin B1 and cleaved caspase-3.
source: We treated both G401 and CLF_PEDS9001_T with nocodazole or RO-3306 for 24 hr and observed accumulation of cells in G2/M as well as increased cyclin B1 and cleaved caspase-3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2d–e) similar to what we observed after treatment with MLN2238.
evidence: The claim is based on cell cycle analysis and immunoblot data after treatment with cell cycle inhibitors.

claim: Treatment with nocodazole or RO-3306 for 72 hr induced cell death in the majority of cells (65–90%).
source: By 72 hr, we found that treatment with either nocodazole or RO-3306 induced cell death in the majority of cells (65–90%) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2f), similar to what we observed when we treated cells with MLN2238 (Figure 4c).
evidence: The claim is based on viability assays measuring cell death after treatment with cell cycle inhibitors.

claim: SMARCB1-deficient cell lines are susceptible to programmed cell death following treatment with a cell cycle inhibitor.
source: These observations suggest that SMARCB1-deficient cell lines are susceptible to programmed cell death following treatment with a cell cycle inhibitor and that the cell cycle arrest observed after treatment with MLN2238 leads to programmed cell death.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing that cell cycle inhibitors cause G2/M arrest followed by cell death in SMARCB1-deficient cells.

claim: The cell cycle arrest observed after treatment with MLN2238 leads to programmed cell death.
source: These observations suggest that SMARCB1-deficient cell lines are susceptible to programmed cell death following treatment with a cell cycle inhibitor and that the cell cycle arrest observed after treatment with MLN2238 leads to programmed cell death.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the temporal sequence of events showing G2/M arrest at 24 hr followed by apoptosis at 48 hr after MLN2238 treatment.

claim: SMARCB1 deficient cancer cell lines required UBE2C for survival based on Project Achilles DepMap 18Q3 dataset.
source: We found that SMARCB1 deficient cancer cell lines required UBE2C, an ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme, for survival.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 loss-of-function screening data from Project Achilles.

claim: SMARCB1-deficient cell lines were in the top 5% of cell lines that required UBE2C for survival (empirical Bayes moderated t-test p-value=0.00016).
source: We noted that these cell lines were in the top 5% of cell lines (n = 485) that required UBE2C for survival (empirical Bayes moderated t-test p-value=0.00016; Figure 5a–b; Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of Project Achilles data comparing SMARCB1-deficient cell lines to all other cell lines.

claim: Cancer cell lines that lack SMARCB1 are dependent on UBE2C.
source: These observations suggested that cancer cell lines that lack SMARCB1 were also dependent on UBE2C.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the Project Achilles data showing preferential dependency on UBE2C in SMARCB1-deficient cell lines.

claim: Gene deletion of UBE2C by CRISPR-Cas9 led to significant viability defects in RMC and MRT cell lines compared to SWI/SNF wild-type or SMARCA4 mutant cell lines.
source: We saw a significant decrease in cell viability in SMARCB1 deficient cell lines as compared to urothelial carcinoma cell line, JMSU1 (SWI/SNF wild type), or non-small cell lung cancer cell line, A549 (SMARCA4 mutant) (two-tailed t-test p-values 4.5e-5 and 4.6e-5; Figure 5c and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is based on CRISPR-Cas9 validation experiments measuring cell viability after UBE2C deletion in multiple cell lines.

claim: UBE2C serves as the E2 enzyme which adds the first ubiquitin to cyclin B1 for degradation.
source: UBE2C serves as the E2 enzyme which adds the first ubiquitin (Ub) to cyclin B1 for degradation (Dimova et al., 2012; Grice et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies documenting UBE2C's role in cyclin B1 ubiquitination.

claim: Cyclin B1 degradation is required in G2/M at the end of metaphase to enter anaphase.
source: Cyclin B1 degradation is required in G2/M at the end of metaphase to enter anaphase (Chang et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation documenting the role of cyclin B1 degradation in cell cycle progression.

claim: RMC models required expression of PLK1 and CDK1, genes involved in G2/M, for survival.
source: Our integrated RNAi, CRISPR-Cas9 and small molecule screens identified that our RMC models required expression of PLK1 and CDK1, genes involved in G2/M, for survival (Figure 3a–b)
evidence: The claim is based on integrated screening data identifying PLK1 and CDK1 as dependencies in RMC cells.

claim: Treatment of RMC cell lines with MLN2238 led to accumulation of cyclin B1 compared to cyclin D1.
source: Treatment of the RMC cell lines with MLN2238 led to accumulation of cyclin B1 as compared to cyclin D1 suggesting that MLN2238 inhibits degradation of cyclin B1 (Figure 5d).
evidence: The claim is based on immunoblot data showing differential accumulation of cyclin B1 versus cyclin D1 after proteasome inhibition.

claim: MLN2238 inhibits degradation of cyclin B1.
source: Treatment of the RMC cell lines with MLN2238 led to accumulation of cyclin B1 as compared to cyclin D1 suggesting that MLN2238 inhibits degradation of cyclin B1 (Figure 5d).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the immunoblot data showing cyclin B1 accumulation after MLN2238 treatment.

claim: When SMARCB1 was re-expressed, cyclin B1 levels were unchanged upon MLN2238 treatment.
source: When we re-expressed SMARCB1, we found that cyclin B1 levels were unchanged upon MLN2238 treatment.
evidence: The claim is based on immunoblot data comparing cyclin B1 levels in SMARCB1-deficient and SMARCB1-restored cells after proteasome inhibition.

claim: SMARCB1 deficient cancer cells require UBE2C expression for survival, in part by regulating cyclin B1 stability.
source: These findings suggest SMARCB1 deficient cancer cells require UBE2C expression for survival, in part by regulating cyclin B1 stability.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple lines of evidence including UBE2C dependency, cyclin B1 accumulation upon proteasome inhibition, and rescue by SMARCB1 re-expression.

claim: Treatment of SMARCB1-deficient cell lines with bortezomib or MLN2238 led to inhibition of the proteasome to a similar extent as in multiple myeloma cell line RPMI8226.
source: We found that treatment of the SMARCB1 deficient cell lines with either bortezomib or MLN2238 led to inhibition of the proteasome to a similar extent observed when the multiple myeloma cell line RPMI8226 was treated (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b; Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is based on proteasome activity assays measuring the ability to cleave a fluorogenic substrate after proteasome inhibitor treatment.

claim: Pulse treatment with MLN2238 caused SMARCB1-deficient cells to arrest in G2/M, which led to cell death as measured by Annexin V/PI staining.
source: We found that upon treatment with MLN2238, SMARCB1 deficient cells arrested in G2/M, which led to cell death as measured by Annexin V/PI staining and led to accumulation of cyclin B1 similar to treatment with a continuous dose of MLN2238 (Materials and methods; Figure 5—figure supplement 1c–f and Figure 5—figure supplement 2a–c).
evidence: The claim is based on cell cycle analysis and apoptosis assays after pulse treatment with proteasome inhibitor.

claim: Pulse treatment with MLN2238 led to accumulation of cyclin B1 similar to continuous dose treatment.
source: We found that upon treatment with MLN2238, SMARCB1 deficient cells arrested in G2/M, which led to cell death as measured by Annexin V/PI staining and led to accumulation of cyclin B1 similar to treatment with a continuous dose of MLN2238 (Materials and methods; Figure 5—figure supplement 1c–f and Figure 5—figure supplement 2a–c).
evidence: The claim is based on immunoblot data comparing cyclin B1 levels after pulse versus continuous proteasome inhibitor treatment.

claim: Treatment with MLN2238 over 26 days induced significant tumor stabilization or regression compared to vehicle-treated tumors (two-way ANOVA p<0.0001).
source: Treatment with MLN2238 over 26 days induced significant tumor stabilization or regression as compared to vehicle treated tumors as assessed by absolute tumor volume (two-way ANOVA test with p-value<0.0001; Figure 5e–f)
evidence: The claim is based on in vivo xenograft experiments measuring tumor volume over time in vehicle versus MLN2238-treated mice.

claim: MLN2238 treatment did not induce significant changes in body weight compared to vehicle-treated tumors (two-tailed t-test p=0.154).
source: and did not induce significant changes in body weight as compared to vehicle-treated tumors (two-tailed t-test p-value 0.154; Figure 5—figure supplement 2f).
evidence: The claim is based on body weight measurements in vehicle versus MLN2238-treated mice.

claim: Mice treated with MLN2238 survived significantly longer than vehicle-treated mice (log-rank p=0.0489).
source: Furthermore, mice treated with MLN2238 survived significantly longer [p-value 0.0489 by log-rank (Mantel-Cox) test; Figure 5g].
evidence: The claim is based on survival analysis comparing vehicle versus MLN2238-treated mice in xenograft experiments.

claim: The tumor that responded to MLN2238 had increased cyclin B1 and cleaved caspase-3 by immunoblotting.
source: We found increased cyclin B1 and cleaved caspase-3 by immunoblotting in the tumor that responded to MLN2238 but did not observe increased cyclin B1 accumulation or activation of cleaved caspase-3 in the tumor without response (Figure 5—figure supplement 2g)
evidence: The claim is based on immunoblot analysis of tumor tissue from mice with different responses to MLN2238 treatment.

claim: The tumor without response to MLN2238 did not show increased cyclin B1 accumulation or activation of cleaved caspase-3.
source: We found increased cyclin B1 and cleaved caspase-3 by immunoblotting in the tumor that responded to MLN2238 but did not observe increased cyclin B1 accumulation or activation of cleaved caspase-3 in the tumor without response (Figure 5—figure supplement 2g)
evidence: The claim is based on immunoblot analysis of tumor tissue from mice with different responses to MLN2238 treatment.

claim: Adequate inhibition of the proteasome was not achieved in mice with a suboptimal response to MLN2238.
source: suggesting that adequate inhibition of the proteasome was not achieved in mice with a suboptimal response.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of biomarker changes (cyclin B1, cleaved caspase-3) in non-responding tumors.

claim: MLN2238 induces a cytostatic response in SMARCB1-deficient tumors in vivo.
source: Combined, these results demonstrate that MLN2238 induces a cytostatic response in SMARCB1-deficient tumors in vivo.
evidence: The claim is based on the in vivo xenograft data showing tumor stabilization rather than complete regression with MLN2238 treatment.

claim: RMC models are dependent upon the loss of SMARCB1 for survival.
source: We have shown that these models are dependent upon the loss of SMARCB1 for survival.
evidence: The claim summarizes the findings from SMARCB1 re-expression experiments showing decreased viability and senescence.

claim: Re-expression of SMARCB1 in RMC leads to a significant decrease in cell counts and a senescence phenotype.
source: Re-expression of SMARCB1 in RMC leads to a significant decrease in cell counts and a senescence phenotype.
evidence: The claim summarizes the findings from viability assays and senescence staining experiments.

claim: Re-expression of SMARCB1 in RMC leads to stabilization of the SWI/SNF complex in the same manner as re-expression of SMARCB1 in MRT.
source: Biochemically, re-expression of SMARCB1 in RMC leads to stabilization of the SWI/SNF complex in the same manner as re-expression of SMARCB1 in MRT.
evidence: The claim summarizes the findings from glycerol gradient experiments showing similar SWI/SNF complex behavior in RMC and MRT cells.

claim: Patients with RMC are often misdiagnosed with renal cell carcinoma due to the rarity of RMC, lack of access to SMARCB1 histological stains, and unknown sickle cell status.
source: Diagnostically, patients with RMC are often misdiagnosed with renal cell carcinoma (RCC) due to the rarity of RMC, the lack of access to SMARCB1 histological stains and unknown sickle cell status (Beckermann et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation documenting diagnostic challenges in RMC.

claim: Conventional targeted exome sequencing may fail to identify patients with RMC.
source: Although SMARCB1 is currently included in targeted sequencing efforts nationwide (AACR Project GENIE Consortium, 2017), our studies along with prior studies (Calderaro et al., 2016; Carlo et al., 2017) suggest that conventional target exome sequencing may fail to identify patients with RMC.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the findings that SMARCB1 inactivation in RMC occurs through intronic fusions not detectable by standard exome sequencing, supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The ubiquitin-proteasome system is a specific vulnerability in RMC.
source: Using genetic and pharmacologic screens in these RMC models, we identified the ubiquitin-proteasome system as a specific vulnerability in RMC.
evidence: The claim is based on integrated RNAi, CRISPR-Cas9, and small-molecule screening data identifying proteasome components as dependencies.

claim: MRT and ATRT models were similarly sensitive to inhibition of the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
source: When we looked more broadly at other SMARCB1 deficient cancers such as MRT and ATRT, we found that these models were similarly sensitive to inhibition of the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
evidence: The claim is based on dose-response experiments and CCLE data analysis showing proteasome inhibitor sensitivity in multiple SMARCB1-deficient cancer types.

claim: Re-expression of SMARCB1 partially rescued the sensitivity to proteasome inhibitors in RMC and MRT models.
source: Re-expression of SMARCB1 partially rescued the sensitivity to proteasome inhibitors in RMC and MRT models.
evidence: The claim is based on dose-response experiments in inducible SMARCB1 cell lines showing decreased sensitivity upon SMARCB1 re-expression.

claim: Proteasome inhibition in SMARCB1-deficient cancer cell lines results in G2/M arrest due to inappropriate degradation of cyclin B1.
source: We found that proteasome inhibition in SMARCB1-deficient cancer cell lines results in G2/M arrest due to inappropriate degradation of cyclin B1.
evidence: The claim is based on cell cycle analysis and immunoblot data showing G2/M arrest and cyclin B1 accumulation after proteasome inhibition.

claim: Treatment with MLN2238 of SMARCB1-deficient xenografts led to a cytostatic response.
source: Although in multiple myeloma cells, tumor regression has been observed in xenografts following treatment with MLN2238 (Chauhan et al., 2011), we found that treatment with MLN2238 of SMARCB1 deficient xenografts led to a cytostatic response.
evidence: The claim is based on in vivo xenograft data showing tumor stabilization rather than regression, contrasted with multiple myeloma results from cited literature.

claim: There have been case reports of one adult and two children with RMC who exhibited extraordinary responses for 2–7 years following diagnosis after empiric therapy with bortezomib.
source: There have been case reports of one adult and two children with RMC who exhibited extraordinary responses for 2–7 years following diagnosis after empiric therapy with bortezomib either as monotherapy or in combination with chemotherapy (Carden et al., 2017; Ronnen et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to case reports documenting clinical responses to bortezomib in RMC patients.

claim: Testing oral proteasome inhibitors such as MLN2238 for patients with RMC and potentially more broadly across SMARCB1-deficient cancers is warranted.
source: Our findings suggest that testing oral proteasome inhibitors such as MLN2238 for patients with RMC and potentially more broadly across SMARCB1-deficient cancers is warranted.
evidence: The claim is a recommendation based on the collective findings from in vitro and in vivo experiments, supported by case report evidence.
